Mr. Ghanshyam Gupta – Interim, Chief Financial Officer  
 
Mr. Rakesh Shinde – Head of Investor Relations

Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good evening, and welcome to the Aavas Financiers Ltd Q2FY27 
and H1FY27 Earnings Conference Call. This conference call may contain forward-
looking statements about the company, which are based on the beliefs, opinions, and 
expectations of the company as on the date of this call.  
These statements are not guarantees of future performance and involve risks and 
uncertainties that are difficult to predict. As a reminder, all participant connections will 
be in a listen-only mode. There will be an opportunity for you to ask questions after the 
presentation concludes. Should you need assistance during the conference, you may 
message the operator. 
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Rakesh Shinde, Head Investor Relations of Aavas 
Financiers Limited. Thank you, and over to you, sir. 
Rakesh Shinde: 
Good evening, everyone, and a very warm welcome to all participants joining us today 
to discuss the financial and operating performance of Aavas Financiers Limited for 
Q2FY27 and H1FY27, along with our outlook for the business.  
The results and the investor presentation have been uploaded to the stock exchanges 
and are also available on our company website. I hope you’ve had a chance to review 
them. We have also uploaded an Excel fact sheet containing historical data on our 
website for your easy reference.  

 
 
Joining me today is the entire management team of Aavas. We will begin this call with 
opening remarks from our MD & CEO Manu Singh. This will be followed by a Q&A 
session. With that, let me now hand over the call to Manu. Over to you, Manu. 
Manu Singh: 
Thank you, Rakesh. And a very good evening to everyone joining us today. It is a delight 
to connect with you during this festive season. On behalf of the entire Aavas family, I 
extend our warmest wishes to you and your loved ones for a joyful, prosperous and 
fulfilling festive period. 
Firstly, it gives me immense pleasure and pride to share that Aavas is on track to cross 
the significant milestone of ₹250 billion in AUM during October 2026, having served 
nearly 4.5 lakh customers. This achievement reflects the trust reposed in us by our 
customers and stands as a testament to the collective hard work, dedication and 
commitment of the entire Aavas team over the years. 
Aavas is embarked on its next phase of growth. The structural demand for affordable 
housing, the depth of the underserved customer segment and our expanding 
distribution, gives us confidence in the long-term potential of the franchise. With an 
established presence across our core markets and considerable headroom to improve 
productivity and deepen penetration, we see a credible path toward achieving Rs. 500 
bn in AUM. 
As we pursue this ambition, the quality of growth will be as pertinent as its pace. Our 
objective is to build a business that delivers sustainable profitable growth through a 
customer first approach, higher productivity, improved operating leverage, prudent 
credit underwriting and disciplined liability management. We will continue to scale 
responsibly, without compromising the asset quality, margins or governance standards 
that underpin the strength of the Aavas franchise. 
Technology will serve as a critical force multiplier across this journey. It will allow us to 
combine the reach and relationships of our physical distribution network with faster 
digital processes, stronger data-led decision-making and robust system-driven 
controls. This should help us improve conversion, reduce turnaround time, enhance 
productivity and deliver a more seamless customer experience. 
Having completed six months at the helm of Aavas, my priorities are clear: to deliver 
sustainable profitable growth through consistent improvements in productivity, 
efficiency and governance. 
During Q2FY27, Productivity per RO improved to 1.2 files / month, compared with 1.1 
files / month in Q1FY27. The momentum strengthened further in September, when 
productivity reached 1.3 files / month. The improvement reinforces our confidence in 
the focused execution strategy, stronger field-level accountability and continued 
emphasis on customer acquisition and continue to lift productivity per resource higher. 
We aim to improve productivity to approximately 1.5 files / month by the end of FY27 
and progressively scale it to 2 files / month.  
The improvement in productivity during H1FY27 was accompanied by a sharp 
improvement of 29% in revenue per RO. This demonstrates that our execution rigour. 
Which is translating into improved resource economics and supporting our objective of 
delivering sustainable profitable growth. Consequently, our Opex Ratio improved by 18 
bps YoY to 3.33% in H1FY27. With further gains in productivity, efficiency and scale, we 
expect to generate stronger operating leverage and progressively improve the Opex 
Ratio to below 3%. 

 
 
We have undertaken a comprehensive review and revamp of our operating processes to 
establish greater accountability and strengthen checks and balances across the 
organisation. We have introduced system-driven controls, reinforced maker-checker 
mechanisms across key processes and implemented rigorous training programmes to 
embed a strong and consistent governance culture throughout Aavas. These initiatives 
provide us with a stronger operating platform to scale the business responsibly.  
At Aavas, People drive Performance. During the quarter we continued our endeavour to 
build a team of people that enables and enhances performance. During the quarter, we 
continued to strengthen our team with the objective of enhancing organisational 
capabilities and execution. Several experienced professionals have already joined us 
across various levels, and we expect to further strengthen the team in the coming 
months. This has given us the platform to drive strategy and execution as we build 
towards the business end of the year. 
These overarching principles are bringing the organisation together around a common 
definition of success. With disciplined execution, continuous measuring and 
monitoring of key levers, plugging leakages, and a strong pipeline of experts leading at 
N-1 level, Aavas is unified in its objective of delivering consistent results. 
Coming to our financial and operating performance, H1FY27 has laid a strong 
foundation for Aavas and highlights the results of our growth initiative. The healthy 
performance during H1 reflects the business is becoming faster, fitter, and more 
productive, with a sharper execution across the organization. 
For H1FY27, we disbursed loans worth ₹35.1 billion, delivering a robust growth of 30% 
YoY, driven by volumes growth. This performance was broad-based and driven by a 
strong pickup in volumes, meaningful improvement in resource productivity. The pickup 
in volumes is derived from gains in productivity and underlying strength of demand from 
affordable housing markets in which we operate.  
Our AUM grew by 16.1% YoY to ₹248.0 billion as of Sep-26. This directly reflects the 
positive impact of our efforts around customer acquisition, productivity, and execution. 
During Q2, our repayment rate normalized to ~17% and will remain in similar range. 
While we still have a long journey ahead, these improvements give us confidence that 
Aavas is well positioned to accelerate growth and deliver more than 20% growth over 
the long term. 
We delivered 16.4% YoY growth in Net profit for H1FY27, driven by a healthy 17% YoY 
growth in Net Interest Income and 18% YoY growth in Operating Profit, supported by 
robust business growth. In addition, improved operating efficiencies, reflected in a 195-
bps YoY improvement during H1FY27 in our cost-to-income ratio, further strengthened 
profitability. 
This quarter was a testament to Aavas’ diverse and strong liability management. Despite 
the volatile interest rate environment, we have kept Cost of Borrowing (CoB) stable at 
7.64%. Following the 25-bps repo rate increase announced by the RBI earlier this month, 
we expect our cost of borrowing to increase. However, we are confident of maintaining 
spreads above 5%. Additionally, we believe the increase in lending rates is expected to 
support yields on incremental disbursements and progressively benefit the overall AUM 
yield. Consequently, we expect our spreads and NIM to improve over the coming 
quarters.  

 
 
During the quarter, we expanded our branch network to 443 across 15 states. In 
H1FY27, we added 21,500+ new customers to the Aavas Franchise. We will continue to 
invest in branch expansion to further deepen and diversify our presence. At the same 
time, our focus remains on ensuring faster branch-level breakeven and closely 
monitoring the performance of newly opened branches to drive better productivity and 
profitability.  
With that preamble, I will now take you through our financial performance. In H1FY27, 
Our Net profit grew by 16.4% YoY to Rs 3.5 bn led by robust 17% YoY growth in NII on 
account of healthy improvement in NIMs. Our Net Worth continues to compound 
steadily, growing at 15.4% YoY, with the strength of our capital position driven by 
consistent compounding internal accruals. Our NIMs remained broadly stable at 7.76%, 
moderated marginally by 5 bps YoY on account of PLR cut, however supported by 21 bps 
YoY improvement in cost of borrowings. Our cost-to-income ratio improved by 195-bps 
YoY to 42.9% in H1FY27, driven by cost efficiency.  
We continue to deliver industry-leading asset quality, with all key indicators trending 
positively and remaining well within our guided range. Our 1+ DPD improved by 18 bps 
YoY to 3.81% in Q2 FY27, remaining comfortably below 5%. Gross Stage 3 improved by 
13 bps YoY to 1.11%, while Net Stage 3 improved by 16 bps YoY to 0.70%, underscoring 
the resilience of our portfolio and the effectiveness of our credit-first approach. Credit 
costs for H1FY27 stood at 24 bps, remaining within our guided range.  
Our RoA expanded of 9 bps QoQ to 3.28% and RoE improved of 28 bps QoQ to 13.63% 
in Q2FY27. We remain focused on delivering quality, profitable growth with strong risk 
discipline and tech-led efficiency, while consistently creating long-term value for all 
stakeholders.  
As I see it, we are at the ground floor of our building, and with a strong foundation and 
an expert team we are confident on the way to building our powerhouse akin to Burj 
Khalifa. With that, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would now hand over to, Ghanshyam Gupta, 
to discuss the financials in detail. 
 
Ghanshyam Gupta: 
Thank you, Manu. Good evening, everyone, and a warm welcome to our earnings call. 
To provide update on borrowings. The quarter closed on a constructive note, with Aavas 
maintaining a stable cost of borrowing despite a volatile interest rate environment and 
uncertain geo-political backdrop. This underscores the strength of our diversified 
liability franchise and strong lender relationships. We continue to enjoy broad-based 
lender support, providing us with access to diversified, long-term, and cost-effective 
funding to support future growth.  
We continued to borrow judiciously, raising around Rs. 16.79 bn at competitive rate at 
7.66% for Q2FY27. As of 30th Sep 2026, total outstanding borrowings stood at Rs. 216 
billion. A well-diversified liability franchise linked with various benchmarks and 
competitively priced, we were able to deliver a 21-bps YoY improvement in our cost of 
funds for Q2FY27. Our average tenure of borrowings continues to be longer than that of 
our assets, ensuring a positive ALM across all-time buckets.  
We have optimum mix of various benchmarks of interest rates such as around 30% of 
borrowings linked to Repo and balance borrowings are linked to other benchmarks like 
MCLR and Fixed Rated Instruments.  

 
 
As of 30th Sep 2026, we maintained ample liquidity, including cash and cash 
equivalents and un-availed CC limits of Rs. 19.6 billion and documented un-availed 
sanctions of Rs. 3 billion. 
Profitability and Capital Position. Our Net Interest Income (NII) for the quarter grew by 
15% YoY in Q2FY27. Our Net Total Income (NIM) in absolute terms grew by 11% YoY in 
Q2FY27 and Net Interest Margin (NIM) as a percentage of total assets expanded by 11 
bps QoQ to 7.81% in Q2FY27. Our disciplined cost management approach, coupled 
with a continued focus on profitable growth, has started yielding encouraging results, 
reflected in a 153-bps QoQ improvement in our cost-to-income ratio to 42.9% in 
Q2FY27. Our Pre Provisioning operating profit grew by 14% YoY to Rs 2.49 bn in Q2FY27. 
Our PAT growth was 10.7% YoY for Q2FY27.  
Our ROA improved by 4 bps YoY to 3.23% and ROE improving by 5 bps YoY to 13.48% in 
H1FY27. We remain well capitalized, with a net worth of Rs 54.0 billion and a Capital-to-
Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 43.77%, significantly above regulatory 
requirements. 
With this, I open the floor for Q&A. 
Moderator: 
Thank you so much, sir. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin with the question-and-
answer session. Anyone who wishes to ask a question may click on the raise hand icon 
from the Participants tab on your screen. We request participants to restrict to two 
questions each and then return to the queue for more questions. To rejoin the queue, 
you may click on the raise hand icon again. We will wait for a few minutes until the 
question queue assembles. We will take our first question. We have Abhijit Tibrewal of 
Motilal Oswal. 
Abhijit Tibrewal: 
Good evening, sir. Thank you for taking my question. Just two-three things. I think during 
your opening remarks, you spoke about improvement in RO level productivity. I think the 
line was a little bad, if you could just repeat that. That was my first question.  
The other thing I wanted to understand from you is, given that this year we have had a 
few states who have seen deficient rainfall. If my memory serves me right, even 
Rajasthan has seen weak rainfall this year. All I am trying to understand is, while we can 
already see the reported numbers, from your experience in the past, how has mortgages 
as a segment behaved during periods of weak monsoon or during droughts? 
 
The only thing I am trying to understand here is, at least the way I look at it, like in COVID, 
I strongly feel that mortgages will remain that one segment where people will still 
prioritize repaying their EMIs vis-a-vis their other loans and obligations. 
Manu Singh: 
Thank you, Abhijit. Yes, I completely concur with the view on a broad-based level that 
mortgages largely remains untouched, even from the present perspective of your 
mentioning about the drought, and shortfall in rainfall. From what we see on our 
exposures, and we have a very keen eye and ear to the ground on these, all my lead 
indicators are actually getting better, as the months are progressing. We do not see, 
currently or in the near future, any stress on this. Parallelly, as a conscious effort over 
time, our exposures to what we call as pure Agri-based income segments has been very, 
very limited.  
Coming to your first question on RO productivity, what I mentioned was while in Q1, we 
had 1.1 files per month as productivity, and for Q2, that has moved to 1.2 files. We ended 
September at 1.3 files, and our go-to aim, this year, is 1.5 files. 

 
 
Abhijit Tibrewal: 
Is it the way we define this productivity is number of cases disbursed per employee? 
Manu Singh: 
Yes. When you say employee, this is the front end level RO, relationship officer, who is 
the actual producer of the file. 
 
Abhijit Tibrewal: 
Sure, sir. The other thing I wanted to understand is have we made any PLR changes after 
the repo rate hike?  
 
Manu Singh: 
No, not currently. We are examining it, and as and when we feel the need of a PLR 
change, we will make it happen. Our ALCO meets every month, and it has a formula-
driven approach towards calculation of PLR. The answer to your question, not currently. 
Abhijit Tibrewal: 
Got it. And sir, lastly, at least what we have been hearing is that on the incremental 
lending that happens, rate will be dictated by how the competitive landscape shapes 
up. We are, of late, last 6-9 months, been hearing even larger HFCs trying to enter into 
near prime and affordable segments. For them, while it is more what banks do and they 
decide to follow, for us, some of it could also be dictated by what the large HFCs who at 
least have a presence in this segment do. Is there anything happening, at least on the 
newer originations? Are they still tracking significantly lower than the back book?  
Manu Singh: 
First point, Abhijit, the way I look at the customer segment that we operate in, is primarily 
very different in ATS from what the larger NBFCs or HFCs look at. Hence, that clear 
segmental difference, fundamentally for me, as we progress ahead, does not put 
competitive pressure from these entities to my target audience.  
 
Second part of your question, whether incremental disbursements are a tad bit lower to 
the book, it is a business cycle. We are confident of maintaining spreads above 5% on 
our placement disbursements, and that is what we are keenly focused on at every 
transaction, which is today on a technology platform called SFDC with BREs as well as 
risk-adjusted returns showing ranges which are very acutely monitored by rank and file 
on which case, based on deviations, needs what kind of rate reduction or rate bump up. 
We are fairly confident of maintaining 5%.  
Abhijit Tibrewal: 
Got it, sir. That is all from my side. Thank you so much, and I wish you and your team the 
very best.  
Moderator: 
Thank you, Abhijit. We will take our next question. We have Chintan Shah from Citi 
group.  
Chintan Shah: 
Firstly, on this transition to 500 billion AUM, under the new leadership team. What would 
be the primary blocks to accelerate the growth from the current 16% levels to 20% level? 
Specifically, how much of this is expected to come from the existing branch vintage, 
versus expansion to newer geographies? What is the expected trajectory of RO 
productivity? I think that is already mentioned at two files. Will it stick to that, or will it 
be higher? That is the first question. 
Manu Singh: 
Thanks, Chintan. Yes, productivity increase per RO and per resource deployed, along 
with expansion, especially deepening into markets that we are currently present in, is 
our medium-term focus. As I mentioned on the branch network, we continue to invest 
in our branch network, to go deeper. Deeper, where there is also flexibility in pricing as 
we go towards the hinterland. Both X-axis and Y-axis, which is where we source, as well 
as per resource deployed and how do we move this up. If a broad math has to be put 
around, this is roughly at about 20%+ CAGR growth on volumes, 8% driven by branches, 
10% by productivity, and about 5%-7% by ATS. 

 
 
Chintan Shah: 
Okay, understand. Got it. Secondly, if I look at our AUM mix and disbursement mix, for 
H1, now we have around 21% of the disbursements towards the LAP portfolio, while the 
share in the AUM mix for LAP is around 14%. Just trying to understand, what is our 
targeted steady state asset-wise mix for HL and LAP? Is that given the higher ticket size 
and yield differential in LAP and also to an extent in MSME versus home loans, how are 
we looking at the risk-adjusted returns, across these segments? 
Manu Singh: 
Steady state on an AUM level, we will continue to look at tending towards, 65-35, HL 
versus NHL. What you see currently is also an outcome of conscious efforts, which the 
teams are moving in. Let me give you a quick heads-up on that. We are very aggressively 
protecting our book. With data and technology, looking at pre-approved offers, we have 
dramatically accelerated offering top-up loans to our existing good customers based on 
the relationship value at near zero cost of acquisition. When we book that, especially in 
Q2 when we accelerated, that goes and sits as LAP. That is one conscious effort which 
helps us both on retention as well as NIM improvement, as well as reduced cost of 
acquisition. 
 
Second, there have been some clearing of the air on what can be classified as HL, what 
can be classified as NHL based on stage of constructions in business as we onboard 
that today. When we look alike between last quarter or last year same quarter, while top 
of the funnel sourcing remains almost identical, booking of anything which would be 
above 60% would fall under the LAP purview. Those are two large shifts which are 
conscious, which show here. Again, repeating, on a steady state basis on AUM, 65-35 is 
where we are comfortable with. 
Chintan Shah: 
Sure. And Sir, one last question, if I may, on the Opex front. Now, given the kind of 
improvements we have seen in the underwriting TATs, digital collections, and agentic AI 
and automation, etc. What is the sustainable Opex trajectory over the next 2-3 years? 
How much further operating leverage can we see from these platforms along with the 
improvement in the RO productivity?  
Manu Singh: 
Our medium-term aim is to get Opex to assets below 3%. The tools that you mentioned 
are not individual, but collective tools, which are running concurrently throughout the 
rank and file. 
Moderator: 
We will move to our next participant. We have Shreepal Doshi of Equirus. Shreepal, 
please go ahead. 
Shreepal Doshi: 
Thank you for giving me the opportunity. My question was, again, on the drought 
situation in some of our key geographies. We have almost 19% exposure in 
Maharashtra, and given our model wherein we are more of a semi-urban and rural 
financier. While numbers are holding up well, are you seeing any incremental pressure 
in October or delays from customers? What would our exposure be to the districts 
where the impact is relatively higher? Sir, if you could give some more color, on how do 
you see things shaping up from here on, with respect to, if it could derail our growth 
momentum also? Thank you for that. 
Manu Singh: 
To answer the second question first. No, I do not see Aavas having any hiccups on asset 
quality at all. On the drought situation, especially the point that you mentioned on 
Maharashtra, we are largely centric around Pune and some of the Marathwada districts 
like Latur, etc. Our concentration is very minimal. Parallelly, I mentioned earlier in the 
conversation that we have been very conscious of steering clear from only agri-based 
income being the basis of our credit assessment. We have always been very cautious of 

 
 
this approach and hence from the perspective of looking ahead from this one deficit 
rainfall cycle, I do not see any impact on Aavas’ book or Aavas’ future growth. 
Shreepal Doshi: 
Got it. The second question is pertaining to your last quarter’s commentary wherein; the 
thought process was to also have maybe a quarter wherein we could see decline in 
spreads so that we could get back to the growth momentum. Are we still open to that as 
a thought process? Or, as you have been highlighting in the call today, that we are 
holding up and focusing more on managing spreads? 
Manu Singh: 
You are alluding to the last conversation that we had in Q1. We have worked very hard 
to make sure that our spread remains above 5%, and as I mentioned earlier, that is 
something that we will continuously maintain ahead.  
Secondly, both levers on cost of borrowing as well as ability to pass on the rate hikes to 
our target audience are both levers that we are actively pursuing as we place 
disbursements today, tomorrow, and the day after. 
Moderator: 
We have Renish Bhuva of ICICI Securities. Renish, please unmute your microphone and 
go ahead. 
Renish Bhuva: 
Sir, just two things. One on this spread trajectory. I understand that we want to maintain 
a 5% spread, going ahead. But when we look at the last three, four quarters trajectory, 
and also when we look at the AUM mix shift, over the last six, seven quarters, it is 
actually tilting towards a non-HL book, which I am assuming will be coming at a higher 
yield. Despite that, obviously spread is coming down naturally, because of the PLR cuts 
we have done in past.  
Now, entering a rising rate cycle, how should one think about the rate cycle? I mean, the 
rising rate cycle should give us a tailwind, or maybe for next couple of quarters, your 
spread would actually first compress and then we will see expansion. How do you 
internally look at the rate cycle which is there currently? 
Manu Singh: 
Renish, I do think that we are now in an interest rate cycle which will rise. While we saw 
25 bps currently, if you look at all the other indicators on tightening at monetary policy 
level, we are in a rising interest rate cycle. What I want us to be very clear about is Aavas 
will always be customer centric, and we will do what is right. Having said that, my 
commentary on spread remains because a larger part of my unit also is here and 
listening. We will maintain above 5% spreads. Tools in our hand are working on cost of 
borrowing. Aavas is a great franchise on the liability side. We continue to leverage that 
proactively.  
Parallelly, yes, a rising interest rate cycle allows right amount of pass on risk-adjusted 
returns to the customer. When I say risk-adjusted returns, it is on product level. Risk-
adjusted return is on credit quality level. Risk-adjusted return is on property type level. 
All of these are available on a transaction basis, governed by technology, and a risk chart 
on which today the team runs on every transaction. So, a diversified retail book on 
placement at risk-adjusted pricing in a rising interest rate cycle, I do believe this 5% is 
sustainable. 
Renish Bhuva: 
Okay. Just to follow up on that, let us say, is it fair to assume that the incremental 
spreads are better than the book spread? 
Manu Singh: 
Almost same today. But as I mentioned, an increasing rate cycle always allows you the 
opportunity on a transaction level to start reversing this trend. 

 
 
Renish Bhuva: 
Got it. But, Sir, because now let us say the large part of our borrowing is floating rate, 
right? So at least whatever part, which is linked to the repo rate, which will get repriced 
in Q3, and since we have not considered any PLR hike, at least in Q3, are we run a risk 
of spread going below 5% is what my worry is. 
Manu Singh: 
Let me answer the second question first. No. Secondly, ALCO internally meets every 
month. We have a very keen eye towards the indicators, and as and when warranted, 
ALCO internally will look at PLR hike. But as I mentioned, the pivot will always be on what 
is right. 
Renish Bhuva: 
Got it. This is very helpful, sir. Just last thing, sort of verification. Obviously, you did 
mention that first half disbursement pickup has been up to the mark, and maybe it is 
slightly better than what we might have earlier thought for. But now, given the 
microenvironment is, do you foresee any risk at all to our disbursement growth targets 
internally? 
Manu Singh: 
No. We are clearly positioned and we are unified in the goal that we want to deliver. The 
trajectory at Q1-Q2, and as we look at October today, is in the right direction. Hence, 
our commitment of growing disbursements upwards of 20% stands. As you know, Q3 is 
a festive season, Q4 is the biggest season, so we will only get bigger and better. 
Renish Bhuva: 
Got it. Sir, so we have guided for what, 16%-17% AUM growth in 2027, right? 
Manu Singh: 
Yes. 
Moderator: 
We will take our next question. We have Kishan Rungta of Emkay Global. Kishan, please 
unmute and go ahead. 
Kishan Rungta: 
Thank you for the opportunity, and congratulations on a good set of results. Sir, my two 
questions are basically, one is on the disbursement breakup, what you have given. If we 
see, there has been some moderation in MSME disbursement, whereas in other 
mortgage loans, we have seen increased disbursement. So how should we look into it?  
Secondly, sir, if you can just throw some more light on the increase in 1+ DPD in this 
quarter. So those are two questions from my side. Thank you. 
Manu Singh: 
On the first one, as I mentioned, our ethos on the book level is a 65-35 split between HL 
and non-HL. Parallelly, what you see in Q2, as I mentioned, has two strong levers which 
are done with strategic direction. First, to ensure that existing customers are offered 
data-backed, technology-driven top-up loans for them to continue with Aavas and 
prevent my leaking bucket. That gets booked as LAP, and hence you see that increase. 
It is a conscious effort, which is right for the customer, right for the firm. Second is 
clarification on what stage of construction can you categorize lending at HL versus NHL. 
So that is the second piece.  
Third, on your question on 1+ DPD, Y-o-Y, we are 18 bps down. 4-bps, which you see is 
largely impact of seasonality. I do not look at that 4-bps, it is like my heartbeat. It 
sometimes goes up, sometimes goes down. As I mentioned earlier, we are seeing all 
lead indicators getting better month-on-month, and we are confident of our guidance of 
credit cost within 25 bps. 
Kishan Rungta: 
Sir, got it. Just a bit more clarification on the MSME side, because if we see, the 
disbursement earlier used to grow at 32% Y-o-Y, whereas in this quarter it is just 18%. If 
you can just clarify that. Are we taking any cautious steps in that segment specifically? 

 
 
Manu Singh: 
I would not call it cautious. It is just about making sure that what we are placing every
